Why we stopped billing by the hour

When we started Fernway Studio, we did what every agency does: we charged hourly.

Four of our first six projects went over budget. Clients were frustrated, we were frustrated, and trust was eroding.

So in 2024 we switched to a fixed price: KES 450,000 per Shopify store.

Clients know exactly what they're paying, we're incentivized to work smarter rather than longer, and relationships are built on trust instead of timesheets.

Since then, we've launched 31 stores. Only 2 went over our 6-week timeline.

1,200 repositories.

When we launched Patchwork CI, we promised it would always be free for open source. Plenty of people told us we were crazy and asked how we'd make money.

Today we run on 1,200 repositories, and about 900 of them are open source.

Here's the part that surprised me most: across all those repos, 1 in 7 CI failures turned out to be a flaky test. That's countless hours of developer time wasted on red builds that weren't real failures.

Open source gave us users, but also data, feedback, and a community. Our most-requested feature, GitLab support, came straight from OSS maintainers, and we shipped it on November 12.

Giving back is strategy, not charity.

#OpenSource #DevOps #CI #DeveloperExperience #BuildInPublic

Losing our first big customer was the best thing that ever happened to Ledgerline.

They walked away 5 months in. It stung.

The reason: they had heavily customized their NetSuite instance, and we only supported standard fields. We weren't meeting them where they were.

So we spent 6 weeks adding support for custom fields. It changed how we think about our customers.

Today we serve 38 customers, and 11 of them rely on custom fields.

That one loss taught us more than any win. When customers push back hard, they're telling you what to build.

What's a loss that shaped your company?

#Startups #SaaS #Leadership #CustomerSuccess #Growth

After 11 years in a clinic, I walked away. Here's why.

I've always loved being a vet, but something kept breaking my heart. Day after day, I'd see anxious pets so terrified that we had to sedate them just to examine them. I knew there had to be a better way.

So in 2023, I founded Doorstep Vet. The idea was simple: bring high-quality care to pets in the one place they feel safest, their own home.

Today, our team of 4 vets does around 30 home visits a week. The pets are calmer, the owners are happier, and honestly, the medicine is better.

We raised our prices by 50%. Here's what happened.

In September, we increased Tabwise's price from $8 to $12 per user per month. It was one of the scariest decisions we've made.

Our support costs per customer had doubled since launch, so the old price no longer covered it. We could cut quality or charge more, and we picked charging more.

We didn't want to leave existing customers behind, so every current customer keeps their $8 price for 12 months.

The result: only 2 of 140 customers churned in the following 2 months.

Your customers pay for outcomes, not software. Price accordingly.

Founders, when was the last time you raised your prices?

We built a mobile app for Rotaship and were proud of how sleek it looked. We assumed restaurant staff would like it.

In the first month, only 12% of staff even opened it.

That stung, but it taught us something: we weren't solving a problem, we were adding one. Restaurant teams don't want another app. They already live on WhatsApp.

So in 2025 we made the call to move everything into WhatsApp. Today it's used across 140 outlets, and the median reply time to shift messages is under 20 minutes.

Meet your users where they already are. Sometimes that means letting go of the thing you were excited to build.

#ProductManagement #Indonesia #StartupLessons #UserExperience

Hardware is hard, so here's our story.

Our first production run at Shelfwise didn't go as planned. 400 labels shipped with a faulty battery contact.

As a young hardware startup, it would have been easy to cut corners. We didn't. We recalled and replaced all 400 labels at our own cost, which set us back about $7,000. Painful, yes. Worth it, because trust is everything.

We also introduced a 100% contact test at the factory. Since then, we've had zero contact failures across 6,000 labels.

Mistakes don't define you. How you respond to them does. To the hardware founders out there: own your mistakes, fix them fast, and build systems so they never happen again.

#Hardware #Startups #Manufacturing #Leadership #Integrity

Title: Show HN: Patchwork CI – Stop letting flaky tests block your merges

Hi HN, we're Tomas and Ines. We built Patchwork CI, a GitHub app for dealing with flaky tests in GitHub Actions. When a test fails, it reruns it. If it passes on retry, Patchwork flags it as flaky and quarantines it, so it stops blocking your merges. It's free for open source, and $10 per private repo per month. We'd love your feedback: patchworkci.dev
